Frog 1
CORE
A frog hops along a row of stones, and every hop costs effort.

There are $n$ stones in a row, numbered $0$ to $n-1$ (the judge numbers them from $1$). Stone $i$ has height $h_i$. The frog starts on stone $0$ and must reach the last stone. From any stone it can jump to the next stone or to the one after it. A jump costs the difference between the two heights, ignoring the sign: from height $50$ to $30$ costs $20$, and from $30$ to $50$ also costs $20$. What is the smallest possible total cost?
the first line holds $n$; the second holds the $n$ heights.
the smallest total cost.
$2\le n\le100{,}000$; every height is from $1$ to $10{,}000$.
Jump $0\to2\to4\to5$: the costs are $|30-20|=10$, $|10-30|=20$ and $|10-10|=0$, $30$ in all. No route is cheaper. Try choosing the cheaper next jump at every stone. Does that rule find this route?

Dice Combinations
CORE
How many ordered lists of numbers from $1$ to $6$ add up to exactly $n$?

Build a list using the numbers $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$. You may use a number more than once, and the list may have any positive length. Count all the lists whose sum is exactly $n$. Order matters: $1$ followed by $2$ is a different list from $2$ followed by $1$.

For $n=3$, the four valid lists are $[3]$, $[1,2]$, $[2,1]$ and $[1,1,1]$. A list containing $4$, $5$ or $6$ already exceeds the target, so it cannot count. More generally, any list whose sum exceeds $n$ is excluded.

Each number can represent the result of one die throw. Each valid list then represents one possible sequence of throws with the required total. We are counting those sequences; we do not need to simulate random throws or guarantee that a real die reaches the target.

The count is huge for large $n$, so print its remainder after dividing by $1{,}000{,}000{,}007$.
one line holding $n$.
the number of ways, as that remainder.

Grid Paths
CORE
Cross a grid from corner to corner, moving only right or down, and never onto a blocked square.

A grid has $n$ rows and $n$ columns of squares. Each square is empty, written \texttt{.}, or is blocked, written \texttt{*}. You start on the top-left square and must reach the bottom-right one, moving one square right or one square down at a time, never onto a blocked square. If the start or the finish is blocked, there are no paths. Count the paths, and print the remainder after dividing by $1{,}000{,}000{,}007$.
the first line holds $n$; then come $n$ lines of $n$ characters each, the rows from top to bottom.
the number of paths, as that remainder.
There are $7$ ways to go from the top-left square to the bottom-right one around the two blocked squares. (Can you find them all?)

Mortal Kombat Tower
CORE
You and a friend take turns beating the bosses of a tower, but your friend needs help with the hard ones.

A tower has $n$ bosses, numbered $0$ to $n-1$, which must be beaten in order. Each boss is easy, written $0$, or hard, written $1$. You and your friend take turns, called \emph{sessions}; your friend has the first one. In a session, the player beats the next boss or the next two bosses: never none, never three. You can beat any boss. Your friend can beat an easy boss, but for each hard boss he beats he must spend one \emph{skip point}. What is the smallest number of skip points he needs?
the first line holds $t$, the number of towers. For each tower, one line holds $n$ and the next holds the $n$ boss types.
one line per tower: its smallest number of skip points.
$1\le t\le20{,}000$; $1\le n\le200{,}000$; all the towers together have at most $200{,}000$ bosses.
One tower. Your friend beats boss $0$ (one point); you beat $1$ and $2$; he beats $3$ (one point); you beat $4$ and $5$.

Fruit Feast
STRETCH
Bessie the cow eats fruit, and may drink water once to make room for more.

Bessie starts with fullness $0$ and her fullness must never go above $T$. Eating an orange adds $A$ to her fullness; eating a lemon adds $B$. There is as much of each fruit as she likes. At most once, at any moment, she may drink water, which halves her fullness, rounding down: $7$ becomes $3$. What is the largest fullness she can reach?
the file \texttt{feast.in} holds one line with $T$, $A$ and $B$.
write the largest fullness to the file \texttt{feast.out}.
